records.source: וַיְהִ֗י אַֽחֲרֵי֙ מ֣וֹת שָׁא֔וּל וְדָוִ֣ד שָׁ֔ב מֵהַכּ֖וֹת אֶת־הָעֲמָלֵ֑ק וַיֵּ֧שֶׁב דָּוִ֛ד בְּצִקְלָ֖ג יָמִ֥ים שְׁנָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And it was after [the] death of Saul, and David had returned from striking the Amalekites, and stayed David in Ziklag days two.
pieces: After the death of Saul, when David had come back from defeating the Amalekites, David stayed in Ziklag for two days.

L.1: And it happened after the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, that David stayed in Ziklag two days.

R.1: Saul was now dead. David had come back from beating the Amalekites in battle, and he stayed in the town of Ziklag for two days.

decisions.choice: the setting: just after Saul's death in battle on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31)
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew tradition 1 and 2 Samuel were a single book; it was divided into two later. This book picks up directly where 1 Samuel ends. Saul and three of his sons, Jonathan among them, died when the Philistines defeated Israel on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:1-6). The opening words echo the start of Joshua ("after the death of Moses", Joshua 1:1) and Judges ("after the death of Joshua", Judges 1:1): a leader's death closes one stage of Israel's story and opens the next.

decisions.choice: David's return from striking the Amalekites: the rescue of Ziklag (1 Samuel 30)
decisions.reason: While Saul was fighting the Philistines, David was pursuing the Amalekite raiders who had burned Ziklag and taken its families captive. He struck them down and brought everyone back (1 Samuel 30:1-20). The two battles happened at about the same time, far apart: Saul's in the north, David's in the south.

decisions.choice: Ziklag: the town in the south that the Philistine king Achish gave David
decisions.reason: Achish king of Gath gave David Ziklag while David was living among the Philistines to escape Saul (1 Samuel 27:6). It was the home of David and his men until he moved to Hebron (2:1-3).

decisions.choice: Saul was now dead. ... in the town of Ziklag
decisions.reason: Readable turns the time clause into a short sentence of its own and says that Ziklag was a town.

records.heading: David hears of Saul's death

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י׀בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֗י וְהִנֵּה֩ אִ֨ישׁ בָּ֤א מִן־הַֽמַּחֲנֶה֙ מֵעִ֣ם שָׁא֔וּל וּבְגָדָ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל־רֹאשׁ֑וֹ וַיְהִי֙ בְּבֹא֣וֹ אֶל־דָּוִ֔ד וַיִּפֹּ֥ל אַ֖רְצָה וַיִּשְׁתָּֽחוּ׃
records.gloss: And it was on the day the third, and look, a man coming from the camp, from with Saul, and his garments torn, and earth on his head; and it was when he came to David, and he fell to [the] ground and bowed down.
pieces: On the third day a man arrived from Saul's camp. His clothes were torn, and there was dirt on his head. When he came to David, he threw himself to the ground and bowed low.

L.2: And it happened on the third day, and look, a man came from the camp, from Saul, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed down.

R.2: On the third day a man came from Saul's army camp. His clothes were torn, and there was dirt on his head to show his sorrow. When he came to David, he bowed down with his face to the ground.

decisions.choice: torn clothes and earth on the head: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: People tore their clothes and put dust or earth on their heads at news of death or disaster. A runner from the battle at Aphek came to Shiloh looking just the same (1 Samuel 4:12), so David can see at once that the man brings bad news.

decisions.choice: fell to the ground and bowed down: deep respect, the honor given to a ruler
decisions.reason: Bowing to the ground was how one honored a king or a great man (1 Samuel 24:9; 25:23). The man comes from Saul's camp and treats David as if he were already king; in verse 10 he calls him "my lord".

decisions.choice: the third day: counted from David's return to Ziklag
decisions.reason: Verse 1 says David had been in Ziklag two days; the man arrives on the next day.

decisions.choice: to show his sorrow
decisions.reason: Readable adds what the torn clothes and the dirt meant (m1), as at 1 Samuel 4:12.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ דָּוִ֔ד אֵ֥י מִזֶּ֖ה תָּב֑וֹא וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו מִמַּחֲנֵ֥ה יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל נִמְלָֽטְתִּי׃
records.gloss: And said to him David, Where from this do you come? And he said to him, From [the] camp of Israel I have escaped.
pieces: David asked him, "Where have you come from?" He answered, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."

L.3: And David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."

R.3: David asked him, "Where have you come from?" The man said, "I got away from Israel's army camp."

decisions.choice: I have escaped: I got away alive from the defeat
decisions.reason: The verb is used of slipping away from danger with one's life (1 Samuel 19:10-12). The word already tells David that something has gone badly wrong for Israel's army.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֥יו דָּוִ֛ד מֶה־הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר הַגֶּד־נָ֣א לִ֑י וַ֠יֹּאמֶר אֲשֶׁר־נָ֨ס הָעָ֜ם מִן־הַמִּלְחָמָ֗ה וְגַם־הַרְבֵּ֞ה נָפַ֤ל מִן־הָעָם֙ וַיָּמֻ֔תוּ וְגַ֗ם שָׁא֛וּל וִיהוֹנָתָ֥ן בְּנ֖וֹ מֵֽתוּ׃
records.gloss: And said to him David, What was the word? Tell, please, to me. And he said that fled the people from the battle, and also many fell from the people and died, and also Saul and Jonathan his son died.
pieces: David said to him, "What happened? Please tell me." He said, "The troops fled from the battle, and many of them fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."

L.4: And David said to him, "What was the matter? Tell me, please." And he said, "The people fled from the battle, and also many of the people fell and died, and also Saul and Jonathan his son are dead."

R.4: "What happened?" David asked. "Please tell me." The man said, "The army ran away from the battle. Many of the soldiers were killed. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."

decisions.choice: What was the word?: What happened? How did it go?
decisions.reason: "Word" here means a matter or event, as when Eli asked the runner from Aphek the same question (1 Samuel 4:16).

decisions.choice: the people: the army in the field
decisions.reason: The word for people often means the fighting men of Israel when they are at war (1 Samuel 4:3-4; 14:15).

decisions.choice: the report builds to its worst news: rout, many dead, and then Saul and Jonathan
decisions.reason: Each clause begins with "and also", so the news grows heavier step by step and ends with the deaths that matter most to David: the king and David's close friend.

decisions.choice: the troops, them (Balanced); the army, the soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: As across Samuel and Kings, "the people" meaning an army is "the troops" at Balanced and "the army" or "the soldiers" at Readable (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔ד אֶל־הַנַּ֖עַר הַמַּגִּ֣יד ל֑וֹ אֵ֣יךְ יָדַ֔עְתָּ כִּי־מֵ֥ת שָׁא֖וּל וִיהֽוֹנָתָ֥ן בְּנֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said David to the young man who told to him, How do you know that died Saul and Jonathan his son?
pieces: Then David said to the young man who had brought the news, "How do you know that Saul is dead, and his son Jonathan?"

L.5: And David said to the young man who was telling him, "How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?"

R.5: David asked the young man who had brought the news, "How can you tell that Saul and his son Jonathan have died?"

decisions.choice: the young man: a young man, perhaps a servant or soldier
decisions.reason: The word means a youth or young man and is often used of a servant or an attendant in war, such as an armor-bearer (1 Samuel 14:1). It does not say what his place in Saul's army was.

decisions.choice: How do you know?: David asks for proof
decisions.reason: David does not simply accept the report; he presses for how the man knows. The question opens the way to the man's own account of Saul's death in verses 6-10.

records.source: וַיֹּ֜אמֶר הַנַּ֣עַר׀הַמַּגִּ֣יד ל֗וֹ נִקְרֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨יתִי֙ בְּהַ֣ר הַגִּלְבֹּ֔עַ וְהִנֵּ֥ה שָׁא֖וּל נִשְׁעָ֣ן עַל־חֲנִית֑וֹ וְהִנֵּ֥ה הָרֶ֛כֶב וּבַעֲלֵ֥י הַפָּרָשִׁ֖ים הִדְבִּקֻֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And said the young man who told to him, By chance I happened on Mount the Gilboa, and look, Saul leaning on his spear, and look, the chariots and the masters of the horsemen had overtaken him.
pieces: The young man who was telling him said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, while the chariots and the horsemen were closing in on him.

L.6: And the young man who was telling him said, "I happened by chance to be on Mount Gilboa, and look, Saul was leaning on his spear, and look, the chariots and the horsemen had caught up with him.

R.6: The young man said, "I just happened to be on Mount Gilboa. I saw Saul leaning on his spear. The enemy chariots and the soldiers on horses were almost on top of him.

decisions.choice: the man's account differs from the narrator's in 1 Samuel 31: he is most likely lying to win David's favor
alternatives: the man found Saul still alive after he fell on his sword and finished him
decisions.reason: 1 Samuel 31:3-5 says that Saul was badly wounded by archers and, when his armor-bearer would not kill him, fell on his own sword. This man says he found Saul leaning on his spear with the enemy closing in, and that he killed him at Saul's own request (verses 9-10). The narrator's account in 1 Samuel 31 is the one the book itself gives as what happened, and the man has an obvious motive: he brings Saul's crown to David and expects a reward. David later says as much: the man thought he was bringing good news, and David's answer was to have him killed (4:10). Some readers have tried to fit the two accounts together, supposing that Saul's fall on his sword did not kill him at once and that the Amalekite then finished him. The text does not say so, and nothing in 1 Samuel 31 leaves room for a second man.

decisions.choice: I happened by chance: the man stresses that he was there by accident
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis: "by chance I chanced". He insists he did not go looking for Saul, perhaps to make his story more believable.

decisions.choice: the chariots and the masters of horsemen: the Philistine chariot force and its horsemen
decisions.reason: "Masters of the horsemen" is a way of saying the horsemen themselves, the men in charge of the horses., the riders. In the narrator's account the men who reached Saul were archers (1 Samuel 31:3).

decisions.choice: and there was Saul ... while the chariots
decisions.reason: Hebrew uses "look" twice to put the listener at the scene. Balanced says it with "there was" and joins the second picture with "while"; Literal keeps both "look"s.

records.source: וַיִּ֥פֶן אַחֲרָ֖יו וַיִּרְאֵ֑נִי וַיִּקְרָ֣א אֵלָ֔י וָאֹמַ֖ר הִנֵּֽנִי׃
records.gloss: And he turned behind him and saw me, and he called to me, and I said, Here I [am].
pieces: He turned around and saw me, and he called to me. I said, 'Here I am.'

L.7: And he turned behind him and saw me, and he called to me, and I said, 'Here I am.'

R.7: He looked behind him and saw me. He called to me, and I said, 'Yes, I am here.'

decisions.choice: Here I am: an answer of readiness to serve
decisions.reason: The words are the usual answer of someone who is called and ready to listen or obey (Genesis 22:1; 1 Samuel 3:4).

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֖י מִי־אָ֑תָּה וָאֹמַ֣ר אֵלָ֔יו עֲמָלֵקִ֖י אָנֹֽכִי׃
records.gloss: And he said to me, Who [are] you? And I said to him, An Amalekite I [am].
pieces: He asked me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.'

L.8: And he said to me, 'Who [are] you?' And I said to him, 'I [am] an Amalekite.'

R.8: He asked me, 'Who are you?' I told him, 'I am an Amalekite.'

decisions.choice: and I said
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text read "and he said", but the form marked to be read aloud is "and I said". The reading form fits the conversation, since it is the young man who answers.

decisions.choice: an Amalekite: one of the people David had just defeated and Saul had failed to destroy
decisions.reason: David has just come back from fighting the Amalekites (verse 1; 1 Samuel 30). Saul lost his kingdom because he did not carry out the LORD's sentence on Amalek (1 Samuel 15:2-3, 26-28; 28:18). Now an Amalekite says he was the one who ended Saul's life.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלַ֗י עֲמָד־נָ֤א עָלַי֙ וּמֹ֣תְתֵ֔נִי כִּ֥י אֲחָזַ֖נִי הַשָּׁבָ֑ץ כִּֽי־כָל־ע֥וֹד נַפְשִׁ֖י בִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And he said to me, Stand, please, over me and kill me, for has seized me the cramp, for all still my life [is] in me.
pieces: He said to me, 'Please stand over me and put me to death, for agony has taken hold of me, though my life still lingers in me.'

L.9: And he said to me, 'Stand, please, over me and kill me, for the cramp has seized me, for all my life [is] still in me.'

R.9: He said to me, 'Come here and kill me. I am in terrible pain, but I am still alive.'

decisions.choice: the cramp: some kind of seizure, agony or faintness
decisions.reason: The word is found only here, so its exact sense is not known. It seems to name a gripping pain or spasm, or perhaps the dizziness of a dying man. In any case Saul says he is in the grip of something that will not let him go but has not yet killed him.

decisions.choice: for all my life is still in me: I am still fully alive
decisions.reason: Saul's complaint is that he is dying but not yet dead. The words give his reason for asking to be killed: he cannot end his suffering himself and fears falling into the enemy's hands alive, as he feared in 1 Samuel 31:4.

decisions.choice: Stand over me and kill me: the request Saul made to his armor-bearer in 1 Samuel 31:4
decisions.reason: In the narrator's account Saul asked his armor-bearer to kill him and was refused. The man's story borrows that request and gives himself the part the armor-bearer refused (verse 6, m1).

decisions.choice: Come here
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "stand over me" asks: come and stand by me, close enough to strike.

records.source: וָאֶעֱמֹ֤ד עָלָיו֙ וַאֲמֹ֣תְתֵ֔הוּ כִּ֣י יָדַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֛י לֹ֥א יִֽחְיֶ֖ה אַחֲרֵ֣י נִפְל֑וֹ וָאֶקַּ֞ח הַנֵּ֣זֶר׀אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־רֹאשׁ֗וֹ וְאֶצְעָדָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־זְרֹע֔וֹ וָאֲבִיאֵ֥ם אֶל־אֲדֹנִ֖י הֵֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: And I stood over him and killed him, for I knew that not he would live after his falling; and I took the crown that [was] on his head and [the] armlet that [was] on his arm, and I have brought them to my lord here.
pieces: So I stood over him and put him to death, because I knew he could not live once he had fallen. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."

L.10: And I stood over him and killed him, for I knew that he would not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that [was] on his head and the armlet that [was] on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."

R.10: So I stood over him and killed him. I knew that he could not live after he had fallen. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm. I have brought them here to you, my master."

decisions.choice: after he had fallen: after he had been struck down in the battle
decisions.reason: "Fall" is the common word for dying or being struck down in battle; the lament uses it again and again (verses 19, 25, 27). The man means that Saul was already wounded beyond saving.

decisions.choice: the crown and the armlet: the marks of Saul's kingship
decisions.reason: The crown was probably a band or diadem worn as a sign of royal office (2 Kings 11:12). The armlet was a band worn on the upper arm. By bringing them to David the man is handing him the signs of the kingdom, and he expects to be rewarded for it (4:10).

decisions.choice: my lord: a title of respect for a superior, here for a king
decisions.reason: The man speaks to David as a subject speaks to his king (verse 2, m2).

decisions.choice: the band; you, my master
decisions.reason: Readable says "band" for the armlet and turns "my lord" into a direct address.

records.source: וַיַּחֲזֵ֥ק דָּוִ֛ד בִּבְגָדָ֖יו וַיִּקְרָעֵ֑ם וְגַ֥ם כָּל־הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And took hold David of his garments and tore them, and also all the men who [were] with him.
pieces: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him.

L.11: And David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and also all the men who [were] with him.

R.11: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them to show his sorrow. All his men did the same.

decisions.choice: tearing one's clothes: the act of a mourner
decisions.reason: Tearing the clothes was the first, sudden sign of grief at news of death or disaster (Genesis 37:34; Joshua 7:6). David does not rejoice that his pursuer is dead; he and his men mourn at once.

decisions.choice: his clothes
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text read "his garment" (one), and the form marked to be read aloud is "his garments". The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: to show his sorrow
decisions.reason: Readable adds what tearing the clothes meant (m1).

records.source: וַֽיִּסְפְּדוּ֙ וַיִּבְכּ֔וּ וַיָּצֻ֖מוּ עַד־הָעָ֑רֶב עַל־שָׁא֞וּל וְעַל־יְהוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנ֗וֹ וְעַל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ וְעַל־בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּ֥י נָפְל֖וּ בֶּחָֽרֶב׃ס
records.gloss: And they mourned and wept and fasted until the evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for [the] people of Yahweh and for [the] house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
pieces: They mourned and wept and went without food until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and the house of Israel, since they had fallen by the sword.

L.12: And they mourned and wept and fasted until the evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

R.12: They cried and mourned and did not eat until evening. They grieved for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and for the nation of Israel, because so many had been killed in battle.

decisions.choice: mourned, wept and fasted until evening: a day of public mourning
decisions.reason: Mourning was loud and public, and fasting until evening set the whole day apart for grief. The men of Jabesh-gilead fasted seven days for Saul (1 Samuel 31:13).

decisions.choice: the people of the LORD and the house of Israel: the same nation named twice
decisions.reason: Both phrases mean Israel, first as the people who belong to the LORD and then as one family descended from Israel. The mourning reaches beyond Saul and Jonathan to all who died in the defeat (verse 4).

decisions.choice: fallen by the sword: killed in battle
decisions.reason: "The sword" stands for war and violent death; it does not mean that every man died by a sword blow.

decisions.choice: went without food, did not eat; the nation of Israel (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what fasting was. Readable says "the nation of Israel" for "the house of Israel" (m2) and "killed in battle" for "fallen by the sword" (m3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶל־הַנַּ֨עַר֙ הַמַּגִּ֣יד ל֔וֹ אֵ֥י מִזֶּ֖ה אָ֑תָּה וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בֶּן־אִ֛ישׁ גֵּ֥ר עֲמָלֵקִ֖י אָנֹֽכִי׃
records.gloss: And said David to the young man who told to him, Where from this [are] you? And he said, [The] son of a man, a sojourner, an Amalekite I [am].
pieces: David said to the young man who had brought him the news, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of an outsider who lives among you, an Amalekite."

L.13: And David said to the young man who had told him, "Where [are] you from?" And he said, "I [am] the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite."

R.13: David asked the young man who had brought the news, "Where are you from?" He answered, "My father was an Amalekite who came to live in Israel."

decisions.choice: the son of a sojourner: a man whose family had settled in Israel without belonging to it by birth
decisions.reason: A sojourner was someone living among Israel who was not an Israelite, under the protection of Israel's laws and bound by many of them (Leviticus 24:22; Numbers 15:15-16). So this man was no stranger to Israel's ways: he would have known who Saul was and what it meant to strike the LORD's anointed (verse 14).

decisions.choice: Where are you from?: a question about his people, not his route
decisions.reason: In verse 3 David asked where he had come from that day. Now he asks about the man himself, and the answer is his family and people. The question is the first step of a trial (verses 14-16).

decisions.choice: sojourner (Literal); an outsider who lives among you (Balanced); came to live in Israel (Readable)
decisions.reason: As across these books, the word is "sojourner" at Literal and "outsider" at Balanced. Readable explains it as someone who came to live in Israel and makes the father the subject.

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו דָּוִ֑ד אֵ֚יךְ לֹ֣א יָרֵ֔אתָ לִשְׁלֹ֨חַ֙ יָֽדְךָ֔ לְשַׁחֵ֖ת אֶת־מְשִׁ֥יחַ יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said to him David, How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy [the] anointed of Yahweh?
pieces: David said to him, "How is it that you were not afraid to lift your hand to destroy {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s anointed?"

L.14: And David said to him, "How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s anointed?"

R.14: David said to him, "Why were you not afraid to kill the king {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has anointed?"

decisions.choice: the LORD's anointed: the king the LORD himself had chosen and set apart
decisions.reason: Saul was anointed with oil by Samuel at the LORD's command (1 Samuel 10:1). Anointing marked the king as the LORD's own, so to harm him was to act against the LORD. David twice had Saul in his power and refused to touch him for this very reason (1 Samuel 24:7, 11; 26:9-11, 23). Now a man boasts of doing what David would not do.

decisions.choice: stretch out your hand: attack, raise your hand against
decisions.reason: The phrase is the one David himself used when he refused to harm Saul (1 Samuel 24:7; 26:9, 11, 23).

decisions.choice: the king the LORD has anointed
decisions.reason: As across Samuel and Kings, Literal and Balanced keep "the LORD's anointed", and Readable says who the anointed one is. Readable also says "kill" for "stretch out your hand to destroy" (m2).

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֣א דָוִ֗ד לְאַחַד֙ מֵֽהַנְּעָרִ֔ים וַיֹּ֖אמֶר גַּ֣שׁ פְּגַע־בּ֑וֹ וַיַּכֵּ֖הוּ וַיָּמֹֽת׃
records.gloss: And called David to one of the young men and said, Draw near, fall on him; and he struck him, and he died.
pieces: Then David called one of his young men and said, "Go and strike him down!" So he struck him, and the man died.

L.15: And David called one of the young men and said, "Draw near; fall on him." And he struck him, and he died.

R.15: Then David called one of his men and said, "Go and kill him!" So the young man struck him, and he died.

decisions.choice: fall on him: attack him, strike him down
decisions.reason: The verb means to meet someone, and in a setting like this to meet him with violence (1 Samuel 22:17-18). David orders the man's death.

decisions.choice: the young men: David's fighting men
decisions.reason: The same word that names the Amalekite (verse 5) is used of the soldiers who served David (1 Samuel 21:3; 25:5).

decisions.choice: the man's death: David's judgment on the killing of the king
decisions.reason: David treats the man's own claim as a confession (verse 16). By punishing it he shows publicly that he had no part in Saul's death and took no pleasure in it. He acts the same way later when Ish-bosheth's murderers bring him their master's head (4:9-12).

decisions.choice: Go and strike him down! (Balanced); Go and kill him! (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Draw near" is a command to go up to the man; Balanced and Readable say "Go" and say what "fall on him" meant (m1).

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ דָּוִ֔ד דָּמְךָ֖ עַל־רֹאשֶׁ֑ךָ כִּ֣י פִ֗יךָ עָנָ֤ה בְךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר אָנֹכִ֥י מֹתַ֖תִּי אֶת־מְשִׁ֥יחַ יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And said to him David, Your blood [be] on your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying, I killed [the] anointed of Yahweh.
pieces: David said to him, "Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth has testified against you when you said, 'I killed {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s anointed.'"

L.16: And David said to him, "Your blood [is] on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I killed {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s anointed.'"

R.16: David said to him, "You are to blame for your own death. Your own words prove you guilty, for you said, 'I killed the king {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has anointed.'"

decisions.choice: your blood is on your head: you are responsible for your own death
decisions.reason: The saying lays the guilt for a death on the one who dies, so that no blame falls on those who carry out the sentence (Joshua 2:19; 1 Kings 2:37).

decisions.choice: David's words come after the report of the man's death but belong with the sentence
decisions.reason: Hebrew stories often tell an outcome and then give the words that went with it. David's sentence was spoken to the man as judgment was passed on him, whether just before he was struck or as it was done.

decisions.choice: your blood
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text read "your bloods" (plural, as in Genesis 4:10), and the form marked to be read aloud is "your blood". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: your own mouth has testified: the man's claim stands as his confession
decisions.reason: David does not try to find out whether the story is true. The man has said in front of witnesses that he killed the LORD's anointed, and David judges him by his own words.

decisions.choice: You are to blame for your own death; Your own words prove you guilty
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom of blood on the head (m1) and says plainly what the mouth testifying meant (m4).

records.source: וַיְקֹנֵ֣ן דָּוִ֔ד אֶת־הַקִּינָ֖ה הַזֹּ֑את עַל־שָׁא֖וּל וְעַל־יְהוֹנָתָ֥ן בְּנֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And lamented David the lament the this over Saul and over Jonathan his son,
pieces: Then David sang this lament over Saul and his son Jonathan,

L.17: And David lamented with this lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son,

R.17: Then David sang this funeral song for Saul and his son Jonathan.

decisions.choice: lament: a funeral song sung over the dead
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun come from the same root: David sang a lament, the kind of song sung at a death, often by professional mourners (Jeremiah 9:16-19; 2 Chronicles 35:25). He sings another over Abner (3:33-34).

decisions.choice: the sentence runs on into verse 18
decisions.reason: Verse 18 continues the account of the lament, saying what David ordered to be done with it; the song itself begins at verse 19.

decisions.choice: funeral song
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a lament was (m1) and ends the sentence here.

records.heading: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לְלַמֵּ֥ד בְּנֵֽי־יְהוּדָ֖ה קָ֑שֶׁת הִנֵּ֥ה כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֥פֶר הַיָּשָֽׁר׃
records.gloss: and he said to teach [the] sons of Judah Bow; look, [it is] written in [the] book of the upright.
pieces: and he ordered that the {{gender:people|sons}} of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow, which is written in the Book of Jashar.

L.18: and he said to teach the {{gender:children|sons}} of Judah [the] Bow. Look, it is written in the Book of Jashar.

R.18: He ordered that the {{gender:people|sons}} of Judah should learn this Song of the Bow. You can find it in the Book of Jashar, a book of old songs.

decisions.choice: Bow: the name of the lament, probably taken from the bow of Jonathan in verse 22
decisions.reason: The single word "Bow" stands after "to teach the sons of Judah" without anything to join it to the sentence. It is most likely the title by which the song was known, as other songs are named by a word in them. Another reading is that David ordered the men of Judah to be taught the use of the bow, since Saul's army had been beaten by archers (1 Samuel 31:3); but the sentence is about the lament, and the words added to make that reading work are not in the text.

decisions.choice: the Book of Jashar: a lost collection of poems, quoted also in Joshua 10:13
decisions.reason: The name means "the book of the upright one". It is quoted for Joshua's words to the sun and moon (Joshua 10:12-13) and here for David's lament. Both are poems about Israel's battles and heroes, so it seems to have been a collection of songs. No copy has survived. The note tells the reader where the song could be found.

decisions.choice: he said to teach: he gave orders that it be taught
decisions.reason: "Said" with "to" and a verb is a command. David wanted the song learned in Judah, his own tribe and soon his kingdom (2:4).

decisions.choice: the Song of the Bow; a book of old songs (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "Song of the" so that the single word reads as a title (m1), and leave out "look", which simply points to the source. Readable explains what the Book of Jashar was (m2), as at Joshua 10:13.

records.source: הַצְּבִי֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עַל־בָּמוֹתֶ֖יךָ חָלָ֑ל אֵ֖יךְ נָפְל֥וּ גִבּוֹרִֽים׃
records.gloss: The splendor, Israel, on your high places [is] slain; how have fallen [the] mighty!
pieces: "Israel, your splendor lies slain on your heights! \q How the warriors have fallen!

L.19: "The splendor, Israel, on your heights [is] slain! \q How [the] mighty have fallen!

R.19: "Israel, your finest men lie dead on your hills! \q How the brave warriors have fallen!

decisions.choice: a lament: a funeral song, set in lines of poetry
decisions.reason: Verses 19-27 are the song David sang (verse 17). It is built of short balanced lines and framed by a cry that comes back three times: "How the mighty have fallen!" (verses 19, 25, 27). "How" here is a cry of grief, the word that opens other laments (Lamentations 1:1; 2:1).

decisions.choice: the splendor: Israel's pride and beauty, meaning Saul and Jonathan
decisions.reason: The word means beauty, glory or splendor (Isaiah 4:2; 13:19). The same letters also spell "gazelle", an animal admired for its speed and grace (2:18), and some read the line as a picture of Jonathan lying like a slain gazelle on the hills. Either way the line mourns the fallen leaders as Israel's finest.

decisions.choice: your heights: the hills of Gilboa where the battle was fought
decisions.reason: The word is often used of hilltop shrines, but here it simply means high ground, the mountain where Saul and Jonathan fell (verse 21; 1 Samuel 31:1). The line is spoken to Israel, whose hills they were.

decisions.choice: the mighty: Israel's warriors, above all Saul and Jonathan
decisions.reason: The word means strong men, heroes of war. "Fallen" means killed in battle (verse 10, m1).

decisions.choice: How the mighty have fallen! (Literal); How the warriors have fallen! (Balanced); How the brave warriors have fallen! (Readable)
decisions.reason: The refrain is drafted afresh at each level. Literal keeps "the mighty", the old and familiar form of the line. Balanced and Readable name who the mighty were, fighting men, using a word that fits both Israel's dead and the enemy warriors of verse 22. The same wording is kept in verses 25 and 27.

decisions.choice: your finest men ... on your hills
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who Israel's splendor was (m2) and says "hills" for the heights.

records.source: אַל־תַּגִּ֣ידוּ בְגַ֔ת אַֽל־תְּבַשְּׂר֖וּ בְּחוּצֹ֣ת אַשְׁקְל֑וֹן פֶּן־תִּשְׂמַ֨חְנָה֙ בְּנ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים פֶּֽן־תַּעֲלֹ֖זְנָה בְּנ֥וֹת הָעֲרֵלִֽים׃
records.gloss: Do not tell in Gath, do not bear news in [the] streets of Ashkelon, lest rejoice [the] daughters of [the] Philistines, lest exult [the] daughters of the uncircumcised.
pieces: Do not tell it in Gath; \q do not spread the news through the streets of Ashkelon, \q or the daughters of the Philistines will rejoice, \q and the daughters of the uncircumcised will celebrate.

L.20: Do not tell [it] in Gath; \q do not announce [it] in [the] streets of Ashkelon, \q lest [the] daughters of [the] Philistines rejoice, \q lest [the] daughters of the uncircumcised exult.

R.20: Do not tell the news in Gath \q or announce it in the streets of Ashkelon. \q The Philistine women would be glad. \q The women of those outside God's covenant would shout for joy.

decisions.choice: Gath and Ashkelon: two of the five chief Philistine cities
decisions.reason: The Philistines ruled from five cities: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (1 Samuel 6:17). Naming two of them stands for the whole Philistine land.

decisions.choice: do not announce it ... the daughters will rejoice: the Philistines' victory celebration
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for carrying good news, and the Philistines had already sent the news of Saul's death through their land (1 Samuel 31:9). Women came out singing to greet victorious armies, as Israel's women sang over Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6-7). David cannot stop the news; the line grieves that the enemy will sing over Israel's dead.

decisions.choice: the uncircumcised: people outside the covenant the LORD made with Israel
decisions.reason: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with Abraham's family (Genesis 17:10-11), and Israel called the Philistines "the uncircumcised" as a name for outsiders to that covenant (1 Samuel 14:6; 17:26; 31:4).

decisions.choice: The Philistine women; The women of those outside God's covenant
decisions.reason: "Daughters" here means the women of a people. Readable says "women", explains "the uncircumcised" (m3), and turns "lest" into plain statements of what would happen.

records.source: הָרֵ֣י בַגִּלְבֹּ֗עַ אַל־טַ֧ל וְאַל־מָטָ֛ר עֲלֵיכֶ֖ם וּשְׂדֵ֣י תְרוּמֹ֑ת כִּ֣י שָׁ֤ם נִגְעַל֙ מָגֵ֣ן גִּבּוֹרִ֔ים מָגֵ֣ן שָׁא֔וּל בְּלִ֖י מָשִׁ֥יחַ בַּשָּֽׁמֶן׃
records.gloss: Mountains in Gilboa, no dew and no rain [be] on you, and fields of offerings; for there was defiled [the] shield of [the] mighty, [the] shield of Saul, not anointed with the oil.
pieces: Mountains of Gilboa, may there be no dew or rain on you, and no fields that yield offerings, \q for there the shield of the warriors was defiled, \q the shield of Saul, \q no longer rubbed with oil.

L.21: Mountains of Gilboa, [let there be] no dew and no rain on you, nor fields of offerings, \q for there the shield of [the] mighty was defiled, \q the shield of Saul, \q not anointed with oil.

R.21: Hills of Gilboa, may no dew or rain fall on you, and may your fields grow no grain to offer to God. \q For there the shield of the warriors was dishonored, \q the shield of Saul, no longer rubbed with oil.

decisions.choice: no dew and no rain: a curse on the place where Saul fell
decisions.reason: In a dry land dew and rain meant life and harvest (Genesis 27:28; 1 Kings 17:1). David asks that the mountains where the heroes died become barren, as if the land itself should mourn.

decisions.choice: fields of offerings: fields rich enough to give grain for offerings
alternatives: fields from which offerings are given
a copying error for some other phrase
decisions.reason: The word means contributions or offerings set apart for God. Joined to "fields", it most likely means fertile fields whose harvest would supply offerings: may Gilboa yield nothing. The phrase is unusual and its exact sense is uncertain.

decisions.choice: defiled: soiled and disgraced
decisions.reason: The verb means to be made unclean or loathsome. The shield lies on the battlefield in blood and dirt, dishonored instead of carried home in victory.

decisions.choice: not anointed with oil: the shield, no longer oiled
alternatives: Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil
decisions.reason: Leather shields were rubbed with oil to keep them supple and ready for battle (Isaiah 21:5). Now Saul's shield lies uncared for. The word is the same as "anointed" in "the LORD's anointed" (verses 14, 16), so the line also brings to mind Saul himself, the anointed king, lying dead. Another reading takes the words with Saul: "the shield of Saul, as though he were not anointed with oil".

decisions.choice: no longer rubbed with oil
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what was done to a shield (m4). Literal keeps "anointed" so that the link with the LORD's anointed can be seen.

decisions.choice: may your fields grow no grain to offer to God; dishonored
decisions.reason: Readable explains "fields of offerings" (m2) and says "dishonored" for "defiled" (m3).

records.source: מִדַּ֣ם חֲלָלִ֗ים מֵחֵ֨לֶב֙ גִּבּוֹרִ֔ים קֶ֚שֶׁת יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן לֹ֥א נָשׂ֖וֹג אָח֑וֹר וְחֶ֣רֶב שָׁא֔וּל לֹ֥א תָשׁ֖וּב רֵיקָֽם׃
records.gloss: From [the] blood of [the] slain, from [the] fat of [the] mighty, [the] bow of Jonathan not turned back, and [the] sword of Saul not returned empty.
pieces: From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the warriors, \q the bow of Jonathan never turned back, \q and the sword of Saul never came home empty.

L.22: From [the] blood of [the] slain, from [the] fat of [the] mighty, \q the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, \q and the sword of Saul did not return empty.

R.22: Jonathan's bow never turned back \q without the blood of the dead and the fat of warriors. \q Saul's sword never came home empty.

decisions.choice: from the blood ... did not return empty: never came back from battle without striking the enemy
decisions.reason: The weapons are pictured as hunters that always come home with their kill: the bow never turned away from the enemy, the sword never came back without blood on it. The fat stands with the blood for the bodies of the warriors they struck down.

decisions.choice: Jonathan's bow and Saul's sword: the weapons each was known by
decisions.reason: Jonathan was an archer (1 Samuel 18:4; 20:20, 36), and his bow is the likely source of the song's title (verse 18). Saul and Jonathan had both won great victories (1 Samuel 11; 14:1-23, 47-48).

decisions.choice: Jonathan's bow never turned back without ...
decisions.reason: Readable starts with the weapons and turns "from the blood ... from the fat" into "without the blood ... and the fat", which says the same thing in plain order.

records.source: שָׁא֣וּל וִיהוֹנָתָ֗ן הַנֶּאֱהָבִ֤ים וְהַנְּעִימִם֙ בְּחַיֵּיהֶ֔ם וּבְמוֹתָ֖ם לֹ֣א נִפְרָ֑דוּ מִנְּשָׁרִ֣ים קַ֔לּוּ מֵאֲרָי֖וֹת גָּבֵֽרוּ׃
records.gloss: Saul and Jonathan, the beloved and the pleasant in their life, and in their death not they were parted; than eagles they were swift, than lions they were strong.
pieces: Saul and Jonathan, loved and delightful in life, \q were not separated in their death. \q They were faster than eagles \q and stronger than lions.

L.23: Saul and Jonathan, the beloved and the pleasant in their life, \q and in their death they were not parted; \q they were swifter than eagles, \q they were stronger than lions.

R.23: Saul and Jonathan were dearly loved and a delight while they lived, \q and even in death they stayed together. \q They were faster than eagles \q and stronger than lions.

decisions.choice: the beloved and the pleasant: loved by others and gracious to them
decisions.reason: The first word means loved, the second pleasant, delightful to be with. The song remembers what was good in Saul as well as in Jonathan, and says nothing of their quarrels.

decisions.choice: in their death they were not parted: Jonathan stayed with his father to the end
decisions.reason: Jonathan loved David and quarreled with Saul over him (1 Samuel 20:30-34), but he fought at his father's side and died with him on Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2).

decisions.choice: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions: speed and strength in battle
decisions.reason: Eagles and lions were the common pictures of swiftness and power (Deuteronomy 28:49; Judges 14:18).

decisions.choice: even in death they stayed together
decisions.reason: Readable says the negative "were not parted" as a positive and adds "even" to bring out the contrast with their life.

records.source: בְּנוֹת֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶל־שָׁא֖וּל בְּכֶ֑ינָה הַמַּלְבִּֽשְׁכֶ֤ם שָׁנִי֙ עִם־עֲדָנִ֔ים הַֽמַּעֲלֶה֙ עֲדִ֣י זָהָ֔ב עַ֖ל לְבוּשְׁכֶֽן׃
records.gloss: Daughters of Israel, over Saul weep, who clothed you [in] scarlet with luxuries, who put up ornament of gold on your clothing.
pieces: Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, \q who dressed you in scarlet and finery, \q who set gold ornaments on your clothes.

L.24: Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, \q who clothed you [in] scarlet with luxuries, \q who put ornaments of gold on your clothing.

R.24: Women of Israel, cry for Saul! \q He dressed you in fine red clothes \q and decorated your clothes with gold.

decisions.choice: Daughters of Israel, weep: set against the daughters of the Philistines in verse 20
decisions.reason: The Philistine women would rejoice; Israel's women are called to weep. The same women had once sung of Saul's victories (1 Samuel 18:6-7).

decisions.choice: scarlet, luxuries, gold ornaments: the riches Saul's victories brought
decisions.reason: Scarlet cloth was dyed at great cost and worn by the wealthy (Proverbs 31:21; Jeremiah 4:30). Saul's wars brought plunder home to Israel (1 Samuel 14:47-48), and the women wore its fine clothing and jewelry.

decisions.choice: Women of Israel; fine red clothes
decisions.reason: "Daughters" here means the women of a people, and "scarlet" is a costly red cloth (m2). Readable says both plainly.

records.source: אֵ֚יךְ נָפְל֣וּ גִבֹּרִ֔ים בְּת֖וֹךְ הַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן עַל־בָּמוֹתֶ֖יךָ חָלָֽל׃
records.gloss: How have fallen [the] mighty in [the] midst of the battle! Jonathan, on your high places [is] slain.
pieces: How the warriors have fallen in the thick of the battle! \q Jonathan lies slain on your heights.

L.25: How [the] mighty have fallen in [the] midst of the battle! \q Jonathan, on your heights [is] slain.

R.25: How the brave warriors have fallen in battle! \q Jonathan lies dead on your hills, Israel.

decisions.choice: the refrain returns, now with "in the midst of the battle"
decisions.reason: The cry of verse 19 is repeated, and the second half of verse 19 is repeated with Jonathan's name. The song turns here from Saul and Jonathan together to David's own grief for Jonathan (verse 26). The refrain is worded as in verse 19 (r-en-1 there).

decisions.choice: your heights: the heights of Israel, as in verse 19
alternatives: Jonathan's own heights, the hills where he fought
decisions.reason: The line repeats verse 19, where Israel is addressed, so "your" most likely still means Israel. It could also be read as spoken to Jonathan: "Jonathan, slain on your heights", the heights where you fought.

decisions.choice: your hills, Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names Israel as the one spoken to, following verse 19 (m2).

records.source: צַר־לִ֣י עָלֶ֗יךָ אָחִי֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן נָעַ֥מְתָּ לִּ֖י מְאֹ֑ד נִפְלְאַ֤תָה אַהֲבָֽתְךָ֙ לִ֔י מֵאַהֲבַ֖ת נָשִֽׁים׃
records.gloss: Distress [is] to me over you, my brother Jonathan; you were pleasant to me very; was wonderful your love to me, more than [the] love of women.
pieces: I am in anguish over you, my brother Jonathan; \q you were a great delight to me. \q Your love for me was a wonder, \q beyond the love of women.

L.26: Distress [is] on me over you, my brother Jonathan; \q you were very pleasant to me; \q your love to me was wonderful, \q more than [the] love of women.

R.26: I am heartbroken for you, Jonathan, my brother. \q You meant so much to me. \q Your love for me was amazing, \q greater than the love of women.

decisions.choice: my brother: my close friend, bound to me by covenant
decisions.reason: Jonathan was not David's brother by birth (though David married his sister Michal, 1 Samuel 18:27). "Brother" is a word of close kinship and of covenant partners (1 Kings 9:13; 20:32). Jonathan and David had made a covenant of friendship before the LORD (1 Samuel 18:3; 20:8, 42).

decisions.choice: your love for me: Jonathan's loyal, self-giving friendship, greater than the love a wife gives
decisions.reason: The word for love is the ordinary word used of friends, family and husbands and wives. Jonathan loved David "as his own life" (1 Samuel 18:1, 3; 20:17), gave him his robe and weapons (18:4), and gave up his own claim to the throne for David's sake (20:30-31; 23:17). David says that such loyalty went beyond even the devotion of a wife.

decisions.choice: distress is on me: I am in anguish
decisions.reason: The word means to be pressed, hemmed in; here it is the pain of grief.

decisions.choice: I am in anguish, a great delight, a wonder (Balanced); heartbroken, meant so much, amazing (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn "distress is on me" into "I am" sentences and choose plain words for the pleasure of Jonathan's company and the wonder of his love.

records.source: אֵ֚יךְ נָפְל֣וּ גִבּוֹרִ֔ים וַיֹּאבְד֖וּ כְּלֵ֥י מִלְחָמָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: How have fallen [the] mighty, and have perished [the] weapons of war!
pieces: How the warriors have fallen, \q and the weapons of war are lost!"

L.27: How [the] mighty have fallen, \q and [the] weapons of war have perished!"

R.27: How the brave warriors have fallen! \q The weapons of war are destroyed."

decisions.choice: the weapons of war: the weapons themselves, and perhaps the fallen warriors
alternatives: Saul and Jonathan, Israel's weapons of war
decisions.reason: The song has named Jonathan's bow, Saul's sword and Saul's shield (verses 21-22), and these are now lost. The words may also be a picture of Saul and Jonathan themselves, Israel's weapons in battle, now gone. The text allows both.

decisions.choice: the refrain closes the song
decisions.reason: The cry of verses 19 and 25 ends the lament.
